extracted.intended_audience: mathematics instructors, math-education researchers, and professional-development facilitators
extracted.subtask_description: Using the EQUIP observation tool and equity-analytics approach to measure, analyze, and disrupt inequities in classroom participation (especially in mathematics) through coded contributions, demographic disaggregation, and iterative professional development cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student contribution (basic unit of analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic unit of analysis for EQUIP is a student contribution. For verbal contributions, we analyze all talk from a single student that is not interrupted by another student. (A single contribution could involve back-and-forth between a single student and the instructor.) As soon as a new student participates, it creates a new contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segmenting observation by contributions allows coding of teacher and student behaviors attached to specific contributions and enables aggregation/disaggregation across students and groups. This definition intentionally captures instructor follow-ups that deepen thinking rather than coding only the initial utterance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourse dimensions (coded features)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coding takes place across a variety of discourse dimensions—features of participation such as the length of the contribution, the type of contribution, the types of questions a teacher asks, how a teacher responds to a student, and so forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EQUIP is customizable so exact dimensions may differ by study; common useful dimensions include length of contribution, teacher question type, and whether students are called on or spontaneously contribute. These dimensions support both quantity and (with added coding) quality analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture multiple participation modalities
rubrics_metrics.description: While many studies focus on verbal talk because it is most public and easiest to capture, EQUIP can capture a variety of participation modalities, including written, gesture, ASL, manipulatives, and so forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any public activity expressing mathematical ideas can be captured with EQUIP; choose modalities to include based on context and instructor needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average contributions / participation rate metric
rubrics_metrics.description: An important metric developed is the average contributions of a particular demographic group (also referred to as a participation rate). Calculate by dividing the overall number of contributions for each group by the number of students in the group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This accounts for different group sizes so comparisons reflect per-student averages rather than aggregate totals. Example: 8 contributions from 4 students → average = 2; 16 contributions from 20 students → average = 0.8.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic data and broad conceptualization of demographics
rubrics_metrics.description: Student demographics are gathered (typically by survey) and conceptualized broadly—any categorical variable that can be put on a survey could be added as a demographic (race, gender, disability, language, major, socioeconomic status, group membership, religion, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Which demographics are used depends on context and instructor needs; because each contribution is coded at the student level, contributions can be aggregated across any demographic variable or cross-sections (e.g., race and gender).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social marker specificity (disaggregate to targeted social markers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any data generated in service of equity needs to be disaggregated along social marker identities: data collected should speak directly to the experiences of the specific social marker (e.g., Black students), not only to equity in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addressing racial (or other) inequities requires noticing, naming, and disrupting racialized phenomena directly; EQUIP's disaggregated data puts social marker identities front and center for meaningful change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customization of dimensions and demographics
rubrics_metrics.description: EQUIP is a customizable methodology—exact dimensions used and demographics included may differ depending on study goals and local context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select dimensions/demographics collaboratively with participating instructors to ensure data are relevant and actionable for local needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding attached to contributions for aggregation/disaggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: All teacher and student behaviors that are coded are attached to specific contributions, which allows contributions to be aggregated or disaggregated across students and groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This design enables answering the who question (who has what experiences) at multiple levels: whole class, groups, and individual students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation and recording practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers typically video record a class session (or virtual meeting) to code it later; real-time coding is also possible under some circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Video recording allows remote coaching, asynchronous coding, and more careful capture of participation. If using a single camera, position to capture student participation; multiple cameras can capture small-group and whole-class interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaling observations for cross-classroom comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing across classrooms, scale results to a common unit length (e.g., the authors scaled results to a 145-minute unit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for variation in observed unit length so averages and totals are comparable across different classrooms or studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on amount vs. quality of participation
rubrics_metrics.description: For simplicity many discussions focus on amount of participation (quantity), though EQUIP can capture deeper levels of detail to analyze quality of participation (e.g., high-level explanatory 'why' contributions, extended contributions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quality-focused dimensions when the research question requires examining depth of reasoning, explanatory moves, or mathematical rigor; quantity analyses reveal broader patterns of access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersectional analyses (race, gender, and other identities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze how participation patterns intersect across identities (e.g., race and gender) because inequities often form complex race–gender hierarchies (e.g., white men more represented and with more high-level contributions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of sample sizes and analytical power when exploring many intersectional subgroups; report caveats when groups are too small for statistical inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional development cycle (observation → coding → feedback → debrief)
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic model for EQUIP-based professional development involves cycles with four main components: 1) observation, 2) coding, 3) feedback, and 4) a debrief meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical engagement aims for 3–4 cycles per semester (meet roughly monthly) with the first meeting about 5 weeks into the semester; iterative cycles allow instructors to set goals, try instructional moves, and measure impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consistent coder to build familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually the same coder will observe the same faculty member throughout the semester to build greater familiarity with the classroom and notice subtle shifts in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency in coding helps detect changes that might otherwise be missed and supports more meaningful feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback reports: disaggregated, qualitative, actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Coder-generated feedback reports should describe patterns of participation and inequity, disaggregate individual and group-level patterns, include qualitative observations, and provide suggestions for changes to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports should enable instructors to set specific, measurable goals for subsequent cycles and identify instructional moves to test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative goal-setting and measuring impact
rubrics_metrics.description: After each cycle instructors set a goal for changing participation patterns and determine specific instructional moves; subsequent observations measure the extent and impact of those practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iterative reflection (3–4 cycles) in a semester can produce meaningful changes; multi-semester engagement yields further improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional strategies to intentionally broaden participation (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete pedagogical moves to bring different students into conversation include: (1) discussing the importance of participation and creating activities to support varied forms of participation, (2) waiting for multiple students to raise their hands before participating, (3) implementing a 'two voices rule' limiting immediate repeat participation, (4) explicitly asking to hear from students who hadn't spoken yet, (5) carefully selecting students to share out after group work, and (6) using turn-and-talk when few/no students are ready to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These strategies helped an instructor shift average contributions by gender over one semester; adapt strategies to local context and goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological caveats and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies using EQUIP may have limitations such as lack of experimental design (cannot claim causality), small sample sizes for particular demographic groups (limits statistical power), and contextual variation across settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report limitations, avoid overclaiming causality, and be cautious when generalizing beyond studied contexts; triangulate with qualitative data where possible.
